The stretch-2 spanner drops both diagonals, shown dashed: each one is replaced by a two-step path, so no distance more than doubles." width="100%"} A spanner is a sparse subgraph that approximates distances in the original graph. For any pair of nodes `u` and `v`, the distance in the spanner is at most `stretch=` times the distance in the original graph: `distance_spanner(u, v) ≤ stretch × distance_original(u, v)` The resulting spanner preserves approximate distances while using fewer edges, making it useful for graph compression, network backbone extraction, and approximate distance queries. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [stretch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Maximum distance approximation factor. Must be ≥ `1.0`. Lower `stretch=` values give better approximations but more edges. Higher `stretch=` values create sparser spanners. [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edge attribute to use as distance in place of the weight field, which every edge must hold as a number; `"weight"` names the weight field. If `None` (default), `weighted=` decides. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, edge weights (`1` where missing) are the distances. If `False`, every edge has distance `1`. If `None` (default), follows whether the graph was created as weighted. Setting `weight_attr=` implies `True`. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducibility. The algorithm has randomized components, so different seeds may produce different spanners with the same stretch guarantee. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with the same nodes but a subset of edges that forms a spanner with the specified stretch. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If stretch < `1.0`, if graph is directed, or if `weight_attr=` names an attribute that an edge lacks or holds as a non-number, or is combined with `weighted=False`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A $t$-spanner is a subgraph $H \subseteq G$ that preserves every pairwise distance up to a multiplicative factor: $d_H(u, v) \le t \cdot d_G(u, v)$ for all node pairs. This implementation uses a greedy scan that considers edges in weight order and admits each one only when the current spanner cannot already reach its endpoints within the stretch bound, costing $O(mn)$ time. The Baswana-Sen (2007) randomized algorithm attains the same guarantee in expected linear time with a tighter sparsity bound but is trickier to implement. The greedy variant here is chosen for clarity and determinism up to the tie-breaking controlled by `seed=`. For unweighted graphs the resulting spanner holds $O(n^{1 + 1/k})$ edges with $k = \lfloor(t + 1)/2\rfloor$, which is optimal assuming the Erdős girth conjecture. Weighted graphs may keep more edges but still dramatically fewer than the original. Spanners are the workhorse behind graph compression, network-backbone extraction, and fast approximate distance queries, and they make an excellent preprocessing step before running an expensive shortest-path or diameter computation. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 5-cycle, a 2-spanner can skip some edges while still guaranteeing every shortest path stretches by at most a factor of `2`: ::: {#0efdbb31 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph() g.add_nodes(range(5)) # Create a cycle g.add_edges([(str(i), str((i+1) % 5)) for i in range(5)]) spanner = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=2.0) spanner.count_edges() < g.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Weighted graphs work the same way -- here a costly direct edge can be dropped if a cheaper indirect route still satisfies the stretch bound: ::: {#91ad45f9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(weighted=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 1.0), ("A", "C", 5.0)]) spanner = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=3.0) spanner.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Raising `stretch=` trades approximation accuracy for sparsity -- on a random graph, a looser stretch bound consistently produces fewer edges: ::: {#623e094a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph() g.add_gnp_graph(n=50, p=0.1, seed=23) original_edges = g.count_edges() spanner2 = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=2.0, seed=23) spanner3 = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=3.0, seed=23) spanner3.count_edges() < spanner2.count_edges() < original_edges ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: :::
